narrative:
The model estimates a 66% chance that you will leave your current job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors that, in combination, signal a higher risk of departure compared to colleagues who are expected to stay.

The strongest influence comes from the fact that you have received other job opportunities while at the company. Most employees who are predicted to stay (77%) have not received such offers; having them makes the model see you as more likely to leave. 

Your total years of professional experience ranks second. With over 11 years of overall experience, you stand out from the majority of stayers, where half have only 1–5 years and just 15% have 11 or more. Extensive experience often correlates with greater external mobility, pushing the prediction toward leaving.

Third, working in the “other” sector also contributes to the leave prediction. Only 22% of employees predicted to stay work in this category, whereas medical and education sectors dominate the stay group. This sectoral difference appears to reflect different retention patterns the model has learned.

Taken together, these three elements outweighed positive signals such as your satisfaction with the work environment, recognition you receive, and sense of job stability. 

The organization should discuss retention measures with you, such as clearer career paths or adjusted compensation, while you may want to reflect on whether the external opportunities truly outweigh what you value here. Addressing these points openly could still change the outlook. (248 words)
